titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
Sustainable energy access is a challenge in Mozambique, Malawi and, more broadly, South Eastern Africa. For example, in Mozambique, currently only 4.29% of people have access to clean fuels, and in cities, people rely mainly on charcoal for cooking. In Mozambique urban citizens still depend on charcoal. Deforestation has been linked to a hike of charcoal prices. The reduction of LPG prizes has not yet translated in a transition to clean fuels.  
However, the lack of available cook stove models means that 1) charcoal cookstoves are of low quality, low efficiency, and produce a lot of air pollution (for those cooking indoors impacts may be unbearable); 2) LPG cookstoves are perceived as being unsafe and unfamiliar to local population. A more sustainable approach entails the design of locally tailored models, built with local resources, adapted to local patterns of energy use, and which provide an additional opportunity for local businesses. The project will focus on design-oriented solutions to deliver access to sustainable fuels in urban Mozambique and Malawi. While there have been efforts to design more efficient charcoal cookstoves, key aspects of safety are seldom considered. Design can help both to improve the safety of charcoal cookstoves and reduce the common incidence of accidents involving children and other vulnerable individuals; and to improve the perceptions of safety of LPGs cookstoves. The introduction of a charcoal-based improved cookstove seems to offer an immediate and effective solution to improve the safety of local residents and evaluate the possibilities to deliver a fuel transition.   
This project builds on research on energy access experiences and needs, led by Professor Castán Broto, funded by the Economic and Social Research Council and the British Academy, and published in several journals.
This programme will contribute to the engineering research base focussed primarily in the developing world and also play a capacity-building role.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
The World Health Organisation estimates that nearly 2 million people die in developing countries due to health issues that arise from inadequate housing (WHO, 2010). Similarly, the United Nations International Covenant of Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, states that adequate housing is fundamental to improving living standards among poor and low-income households. Without adequate shelter, families lack security and are vulnerable to natural disasters and the chaos of civil conflict (UN,2010). 
These examples clearly illustrate the need for adequate housing and hence, scientific research into the development of cost-effective, sustainable housing for developing countries. The developed world is making significant progress in tackling this challenge however, in many other parts of the world, there is still a great need for low cost, robust and thermally comfortable housing. In addition to the adequate housing requirement, energy access, water and sanitation are still major problems in many rural communities.
This project proposes to address some of these pressing issues by using a multidisciplinary approach in empowering local capacity to use new methods and locally engineered materials, in building, low cost, self-sufficient,  modular-homes.  The design of the homes will incorporate upcycled materials and local agricultural waste that would have been otherwise incinerated or dumped. For example, walls could be made of plastic bottles, and wall/floor boards could be a composite made from agricultural waste such as sugarcane, coconut shells and/or banana stems. The building will also incorporate Energy and water harvesting facilities. The multi-disciplinary nature of this project will ensure that structural, energy, aesthetic and economic performance of the building are optimized. 
The activities of the project will include  fabricating and testing  various composites materials manufactured from plastics and agricultural waste. It will also explore various options for integrating energy, water and sanitation measures.

descriptions: Nepal is a low income country where the majority of people live in chronic poverty, and their situation is exacerbated by the disasters (in particular earthquakes) that regularly hit the country. Nepal has comprehensive building codes and a Building Act with accompanying bylaws to reinforce and support the implementation of the building codes and standards. A major engineering research challenge exists however, as both the existing building stock is refurbished and the new stock continuously added by the informal construction sector. Nepal is a country with dense urban areas, most of which have been constructed informally, without adherence to any building standards and codes. Such informal construction leaves urban areas highly vulnerable and with little resilience to any disaster. This situation is not unique to Nepal’s urban areas, as rapid urbanisation in many developing countries has similarly led to a boom in informal construction sectors and construction that has little regard for building codes and regulations. This project aims to explore the pathways of engaging the informal construction sector in appreciating the importance of hazard-resilient buildings, and to enhance awareness of resilience among the informal construction professionals in urban Nepal. This funding will establish a foundation for strategic GCRF research in the areas of resilient urban housing stock; decision-making support for the informal construction sector; and bottom-up approaches for promoting resilient urban areas of Nepal and other ODA countries.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Engineering for Development Research Fellowships
descriptions:
Within the fine chemicals, agrochemicals and pharmaceutical industries, crystallisation is the most frequently used separation process in the manufacturing of solid particles. Apart from providing well-defined solid particles, it offers the possibility of product purification. Typical pharmaceutical products, for example, must be produced at purity levels >99.9% using crystallisation.
However, the attainable purity depends strongly on the host/impurity system and is the result of kinetic and structural factors (e.g., solid solution formation). This often limits the effectiveness of crystallisation as a purification process, often leading to costly multi-step processes. This drawback especially impacts manufacturers of off-patent pharmaceuticals, which are often based in ODA-eligible countries, since margins are low for these products and manufacturing processes account for the majority of costs.
This fellowship will deliver a new way to accomplish targeted design of more efficient production processes, thereby decreasing costs of off-patent pharmaceuticals and increasing competitiveness of pharmaceutical manufacturers in ODA-eligible countries.
Crystals grow as well-ordered structures with faceted shapes related to the underlying symmetry of the crystal. Each facet is a termination of the crystal structure and exposes a unique set of chemical functionalities to the environment. For different facets, this results in different growth rates and abilities to accept/reject impurities present in the solution (Figure 1). Impurity incorporation is therefore inherently anisotropic, which has been neglected in previous studies focussing on overall distribution coefficients of impurities between crystal and mother liquor (Figure 2). A step change in process design capabilities for enhanced purity requires a molecular scale approach/understanding. Recent advances in surface analysis techniques and molecular simulations enable investigating the precise factors influencing impurity incorporation/rejection in a facet-specific manner.
This fellowship combines such detailed measurements and simulations with a multi-scale modelling approach ranging from the molecular to the process scale. Combining these aspects will lead to ‘first-principles’-based process design strategies, enabling cheaper production of highly pure products.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Engineering for Development Research Fellowships
descriptions:
The leading cause of childhood mortality in sub-Saharan Africa is malaria, of which cerebral malaria is the most severe neurological complication. If diagnosed and treated, around 80% of children can survive, but more than 25% will suffer long-term neurological consequences, such as impaired cognition and motor function, and epilepsy. In developing countries in Asia and Latin America, perinatal complications such as birth asphyxia have overtaken communicable diseases as the principal causes of morbidity in children under five.
In each of these leading causes of death and disability, a key factor is impaired oxygen delivery to the brain. Neurological damage due to insufficient oxygen delivery is made more likely due to the increased metabolic demand which occurs during seizure activity, which is a common occurrence amongst those suffering from brain injury, and can itself be a source of further traumatic brain injury.
The lack of low-cost portable instrumentation for neurological monitoring of neonates and children in the developing world restricts our ability to diagnose and monitor the progression of such diseases, to effectively develop new treatments, and to target the use of scarce rehabilitatory resources.
To satisfy this unmet need, I propose the development and implementation of an accessible technology which is capable of measuring blood flow and oxygenation status with high spatial resolution, unique in providing a non-invasive, low-cost and portable means to study and monitor the progression of diseases such as cerebral malaria, and the encephalopathies which result from perinatal complications.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Engineering for Development Research Fellowships
descriptions:
Infectious diseases are one of the greatest challenges facing developing countries today. Control of HIV/AIDS, malaria, tuberculosis and other major communicable diseases is one of the eight Millennium Development Goals set out by the United Nations, and is part of its ambitious post-2015 development agenda. The World Health Organisation estimates that in Africa alone 450,000 people die of tuberculosis each year, and drug resistant strains are on the rise globally.  Dame Sally Davies, Chief Medical Officer for England, has described the threatened loss of antibiotics to the world as on a par with climate change. Currently, tuberculosis tests take up to two months, and require a laboratory with highly-trained microbiologists. With single-molecule microbial genome sequencing techniques, test results can be obtained within a day, drastically reducing the time required to begin treatment specific to the microbial strain. If genome-sequencing devices were to be made available to local health centres in developing countries this could save millions of lives, reduce the cost of healthcare, and prevent the spread of drug resistant infections.
DNA sequencing is a rapidly evolving methodology to read the sequence of bases in a genome. Single-molecule sequencing techniques allow the identification of infectious agents, detection of drug resistance, and improvements in outbreak surveillance. I propose to use my unique research expertise in single-molecule electronics to understand and pioneer a new generation of graphene-based sequencing devices, which will offer faster, cheaper, and more reliable DNA sequencing. Graphene can be grown cheaply in large amounts, enabling cost-effective mass-production of these devices, while its unique properties – atomically thin, ultra-high conductivity, compatibility with organic and inorganic materials and highly flexible – offer the prospect of reliable device performance, even under harsh conditions.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Engineering for Development Research Fellowships
descriptions:
According to the World Health Organisation[1], 63% of all deaths annually occur due to noncommunicable
or chronic diseases, principally cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and cancer.
These are the most frequent causes of mortality in developing countries. Nearly two-thirds of
all cancer deaths occur in low- and middle-income countries. Lung, breast, stomach and liver
cancers cause the majority of cancer deaths. For cancers, mortality is high, and survival rates
are low because the majority remain undiagnosed, or diagnosed too late for effective
treatment. Without any changes in underlying risk, the absence of cost-effective diagnostic
techniques may lead to an increase in mortality rates of more than 80% in low-income
countries in 10years. The geographical variation in cancer types distribution and patterns in the
Africa[2] and South-East Asia[3] demonstrates the urgent requirement for universal diagnostic
techniques in all regions as the first step in effective cancer care.
The project will meet the developing countries’ medical challenges by offering new costeffective
diagnostic technologies and design tools for highly sensitive, in-vivo label-free imaging
of diseased and healthy tissues. The fabrication of ultrafast mid-infrared fibre laser systems is
straightforward, does not require clean-room facilities and, therefore, decreases the cost
compared with existing diagnostic techniques. Fibre laser systems feature low maintenance
cost and alignment-free operation, and so do not require professionally trained operators.
Fourier transform infrared spectrometers or Raman spectrometers with multiple nonlinear
signal enhancement and complex analysis techniques can be replaced with a single compact
device. Novel technologies will not only reduce up-front costs but will also cut running costs by
greatly reducing power consumption. Also, direct measurement of molecular fingerprints in
biological tissues potentially allows an increase in sensitivity.
This project combines the key areas of research on ultrafast pulse light sources, nonlinear
techniques, dispersion-management technologies and spectroscopy in which it is vital for the
UK to retain its leadership. The UK remains a global research heavyweight in biological sciences
and environmental science and holds a leading position regarding article citations in
mathematics, physical sciences and engineering. The Fellow is an independent and mature
researcher with a truly translational background who is able to commit a significant and longterm
research effort to the project’s objectives. The project will be synergetic with other
projects at Aston University in engineering, and the physical and medical sciences.
Additional GCRF funding will help the Fellow develop an affordable tool to spread out across
the globe and extend the database of tested biotissues, hence creating an accurate
discrimination model. It will also allow the Fellow to attend conferences focused on the
challenges of developing countries, which bring together professionals from international
communities, and meet stakeholders and leaders in government. The main stakeholders will be
identified to discuss cancer-related matters, understand the aspects of introducing new
equipment and the possibility of local funding for translation of the proposed research to
developing countries.

Within urban centres of ODA countries, reinforced concrete structures (RCS) are the most common building archetype. However, poor design and poor quality control during construction make RCSs more susceptible to earthquake damage compared to other building systems. In addition, ODA countries possess limited numbers of engineers qualified to undertake post-earthquake damage assessment and delays in the completion of damage assessments can be significant. Without a building damage assessment, victim communities are unable to recover from the earthquake event and, on top of the physical damage, delays can lead to significant additional social and economic damage within the community. 
This proposal aims to develop a Post-Earthquake Structural Health Monitoring System (PE-SMS). The PE-SMS will be an end-to-end proof of concept wireless sensor network for collection, communication and aggregation of structural health data. This data will greatly facilitate the post-earthquake structural assessment process, helping engineers target buildings that show signs of distress and allow some form of social and economic recovery in advance of the completion of a full damage assessment. 
The PE-SMS will be validated through lab tests in the UK and field trials in the Philippines where a recent earthquake will provide a sample of buildings to test the system. These trials aim to show that wirelessly connected battery powered sensors are feasible and practical, for post-earthquake evaluation. A PE-SMS system deployed quickly will have a significant impact, reducing delays in the damage assessment process, reducing potential loss of life due to building collapse and mitigating avoidable social and economic losses. 
The PE-SMS proposal will culminate in a five-day research workshop. This workshop will allow us to disseminate our research to local scientists and government bodies and provide opportunities for researcher development at our ODA partner in the Philippines.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions: Somalia is one of the poorest countries in the world, devastated by conflict and recurring weather-induced disasters. Limited water availability during long and intense dry seasons puts severe pressure on water resources and forces communities into frequent displacement. To cope with these droughts, local and international humanitarian organisations, government agencies, and others, invest large amounts of resources to mitigate such events. For example, Concern Worldwide provides households with emergency cash support to help them meet basic needs and support their fragile local economies. Emergency aid, inevitably, produces local competition to access its limited support and leads to false-reporting of water scarcity. To optimise the delivered resources, a better quantification of water availability and its role in driving social dynamics is needed. However, as is common in many regions in the world where insecurity, socioeconomic development and environmental change are the strongest, Somalia is acutely data-scarce. The necessary information could be collected, in principle, by simple measurements of key components of the water cycle, such as groundwater levels in shallow wells. But because of irregular data collection intervals and eventual bias in manual observations due to potential conflict of interests, autonomous, automatic, objective, and continuous measurements are required. Recent technological developments, particularly the advent of cheap and reliable environmental sensors, enable cost-effective and robust hydrological monitoring. These, in combination with other upcoming technologies such as remote sensing and wireless transmission, for example, in the context of the Internet of Things, holds promise for improved data collection, transmission, curation, process and knowledge generation. This project will design and develop environmental sensor prototypes based on novel and upcoming technologies; subsequently, deploy a small water level monitoring network in field conditions; and lastly, process, analyse, and use the generated data to optimise the intervention of development and humanitarian organisations.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
This research project brings together academics from multiple disciplines (engineering, quality management, logistics, business and economics) with Ugandan women’s groups in order to identify the critical factors for building manufacturing capability for the craft women of Uganda.
According to the report on Women’s entrepreneurship Development in Uganda by the International Labour Organisation, women make up 52.5% of the labour force and are an important pool of potential talent to help Uganda meet its development goals. However, it is generally known that women face more challenges than men in starting, managing and growing their enterprises. They are more disadvantaged than men due to legal impediments, established cultural norms and attitudes about women’s roles, less mobility, and the unequal demands of domestic responsibilities on women’s time.
Making a living through craft products such as jewellery, weaving and baby sacks is an established and often the only way that families can survive. It is a predominantly female trade with the skills passed from generation to generation in an informal and unstructured way (Boonabaana, 2016)
We want to establish a pilot by working with the local women of Uganda and have a knowledge exchange that it will transform this informal craft making process into a manufacturing process. This will enable women to manufacture products cheaper, faster, market them in a wider area and perhaps start exporting to other countries. Manufacturing operations might bring to mind industrial equipment. The principles however that any manufacturing process is based are the same regardless of the size or the volume of the products. Inventory, supply chain, quality management, economics and sustainability are in every manufacturing company. The participants of this project will work with the local communities to enhance their knowledges of these elements with the aim to build a level of industrial capacity.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
Hand foot and mouth disease (HFMD) and tetanus are serious infectious diseases in the developing world. Tetanus is a severe disease requiring long periods of intensive care treatment and often with a high mortality. HFMD affects large numbers of infants and young children throughout South-East Asia. In Ho Chi Minh City (Vietnam) alone, between 3,000 and 10,000 cases are seen every year.  In both diseases the main cause of death is “autonomic nervous system dysfunction” (ANSD), resulting in disturbance of blood pressure and heart rate which is often only apparent too late for effective treament. As the autonomic nervous system determines heart rate, there exists the potential for providing early detection of ANSD using machine learning methods applied to physiological data acquired from ICU patients.  Such early warning would have a transformative effect on how the two diseases are identified and treated in developing regions.
We aim to develop a system to assist ANDS detection using a multivariate monitoring system using physiological data This will be a low-cost application suitable for resource-limited settings where the majority of tetanus and HFMD occurs.
In Vietnam, current policy requires that most children with HFMD are admitted to hospital to identify those with severe disease at an early stage. However, as only a small proportion of cases progress to severe disease and ANSD, this approach results in enormous healthcare costs. Intelligent, early prediction of those with ANSD would mean fewer children require hospital admission and allow better allocation of resources in developing nations. In tetanus, ANSD detection and prediction would allow early detection and more effective treatment. In addition, patients with these diseases are often given antibiotics, thus a robust and reliable predictive system would also reduce unnecessary antibiotic use (and the consequent spread of antimicrobial resistance, a major threat to global public health).

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
Dengue is an emerging infectious disease affecting over 60 million people a year, mainly in developing countries. At the Hospital for Tropical Diseases Ho Chi Minh City over 100 dengue cases present each day thus the disease causes significant healthcare burden. Dengue causes fluid leakage from the blood vessels into tissues resulting in low blood pressure and shock. Treatment consists of intravenous fluid to replace fluid leakage and restore blood pressure. Estimating the degree of fluid leakage is essential for good clinical management as giving too much or too little fluid may be harmful. Fluid leakage into tissues means conventional methods of assessment of fluid requirements are inaccurate and the only alternatives are invasive and expensive systems requiring significant training and expertise and thus not suitable for the majority of settings where dengue occurs. 
The Mobile Health Systems Lab at ETH Zurich has developed a sensor based mobile health (mHealth) dehydration management framework called AMBICA (Accurate Model for Bio-Composition Analysis). AMBICA is designed for appropriate triage and monitoring of dehydration non-invasively in infants and young children at health centres. The benefit of this technology is that it can perform a continuous measurement of fluid status during rehydration therapies and display trend changes. In this project, we aim to adapt this technology to perform spectral bio-composition analysis on adults and children. This adaptation would enable measurements on dengue patients and assist in the determination of fluid requirements. 
This application is for a proof-of-principal project to develop devices and perform preliminary evaluation in order to assess the feasibility and gain the necessary data to plan and fund a larger scale clinical trial.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
A key challenge in delivering sustainable energy projects in rural communities is the incorporation of social complexities in the design, implementation and operation phase. Solar Energy electricity generation has seen dramatic cost reductions and is thus ideally placed to provide the energy required for social and economic development in rural communities. This allows rural communities the productive use of electricity and a reduction of energy poverty. However, in order for rural energy projects to be successful the local context and complexities must be carefully considered. This includes issues of collaborative development, cultural and behavioural factors, informal settlings, community ownership and economic inclusion. These issues must be considered at the early project development stage, in close collaboration with local stakeholders. 
The conventional engineering approach focusses on the technical and economic feasibility of energy projects. This project will bring together researchers and practitioners in the disciplines of reliability engineering, solar energy technology and social development research. The aim is to develop an applied methodology that will enhance the social planning and economic inclusion of communities for rural energy projects. This will be achieved through a planning tool, facilitating a social Due Diligence process. 
The programme of activities includes stakeholder workshops to develop the social risk assessment methodology, applied to the 100kW rural PV project developed by Borena Energy in Doornkop Farm, South Africa. The project will also enable ‘Engineers without Borders’ to provide two to test and implement the new methodologies for early-stage. 
A successful pilot project will improve the Due Diligence practise of PV projects, enhancing the long-term resilience and sustainability of energy projects and thus benefitting the rural communities, project developers, such as Borena Energy and project investors.  It is also envisaged that the developed and tested approach will be applicable to low-carbon technologies in other developing countries.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
Solar power has the potential to enhance the lives of countless rural community that are not connected to a national grid. Individual solar panel systems installed on every home require large infrastructure investment, and  considerable  space to physically locate the panels. Local Community power sources can remove this burden on individuals in terms of cost, and space requirements for installation. A small centralised solar power source can readily be developed using Mirrors, called heliostats, that concentrate solar irradiation to a single receiver where it is converted to thermal energy. Heliostats require highly accurate optics to ensure that the reflected light intercepts the receiver and does not damage the surrounding structure. A system with hundreds of heliostats thus requires regular calibration to ensure that pointing accuracy is maintained. Conventionally, heliostats are calibrated individually which requires a timeous process. This research proposes the development of a triangulation sensor system that can be placed on the heliostat to enable autonomous calibration, though the use of automotive parking sensors, will be investigated in a triangulation system. Our calibration system will be tested on a  400kW Heliostat power station, that uses a micro gas turbine central receiver system.
Initial component tests in regards of sensor accuracy, maximum sensing distance and minimum position resolution will be evaluated and combined with a tracking test system demonstration in a controlled environment. A sensor system integration and packaging for remote and harsh environments will be subsequently investigated and developed. The final project step will include an initial system demonstrator test on a functioning heliostat test site. 
The autonomous calibration will remove the current limitation on the number of heliostats, enable more regular calibration, increasing the system efficiency, and will improve the techno-economic viability of the technology to increase the technology potential and possible uptake in rural and remote environments.

agency: Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
titles: Frontiers of Engineering for Development
descriptions:
Management of water is one of the most important factors that will shape sustainable development. Adoption of decentralised infrastructure solutions is seen as a means of achieving this goal. This is particularly true for South Africa, where 55.9 million people are currently exposed to severe drought. Eco-V has developed a novel GreenTower Microgrid technology that efficiently harvests and stores energy from the environment. However, the challenge remains how this technology can be transferred through innovation on traditional projects to enable greywater recycling with optimal quality, cost of installation and maintenance including real-time control. 
This project will set-up a small-scale pilot for social housing in Pretoria to combine the environmental, civil, electronic and mechanical engineering expertise of project partners in developing a new Blue-GreenTower state-of-art water and renewable energy solution. The system aims to recover up to 75% of domestic greywater to a sufficient standard for bathing. Furthermore, local groundwater will be used to replenish the bath water supply. Monitoring equipment will be installed to assess the performance of the system, and data obtained will be used to develop a simulation model of the pilot scheme. The results will be used as a proof of concept and to assess the potential of the technology to significantly reduce pressures on city infrastructure and CO2 emissions. 
Outcomes from this project will directly benefit 80 local residents by increasing their resilience to drought and reducing their water and energy costs by £4,500 per year. It will serve as a showcase for the municipality who carries the burden of aging infrastructure, and open the possibilities for wider dissemination across the continent supported by the African Development Bank. Finally, the project addresses global challenges of water scarcity and energy efficiency, in which the UK scientists are both thought-leaders and technology pioneers.
This programme will contribute to the engineering research base focussed primarily in the developing world and also play a capacity-building role.
